hints: Compare the two shapes on the graph - where the line is still climbing steeply versus where it has gone flat - and think about what each shape tells you about whether extra light still makes a difference.
walkthrough:
Link Shape to Limiting Idea**
When the curve is rising, increasing light intensity on the x-axis gives a higher rate of photosynthesis on the y-axis. That tells you light supply is holding the rate back at that point.

Contrast With the Plateau**
Once the curve is flat, adding more light gives no further increase, so something else such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature must be limiting. So X belongs on the early rising part, not on the flat part.
Final answer: X placed anywhere on the rising sloping part of the curve, to the left of where the curve levels to a plateau.

hints: Think about the direction of information flow here - you are starting with mRNA and making DNA, which is the reverse of normal transcription, so which viral enzyme does this job?
walkthrough:
Remember What cDNA Means**
 cDNA is complementary DNA made as a DNA copy of an mRNA molecule. Normal transcription makes RNA from DNA, so this is the opposite direction.

Name the Reverse Enzyme**
The enzyme that synthesises DNA using an RNA template is reverse transcriptase, first found in retroviruses such as HIV and now used in the lab to make cDNA for microarrays.

hints: Focus on the first step of gene expression - switching transcription on or off at the promoter - and recall what type of protein binds to DNA near the promoter to do this.
walkthrough:
Locate Control at Transcription**
Genes are switched on when RNA polymerase can bind the promoter and transcribe mRNA. In plants, as in animals, this is regulated by proteins that bind to specific DNA sequences.

Name the Regulators**
These DNA-binding regulatory proteins are transcription factors. Activators increase transcription, repressors decrease it, allowing light signals to change which kale genes are expressed.

hints: Start from Fig. 8.1 - if high light allows a much faster rate of photosynthesis than low light, what does the plant need more of to run all those light-dependent and Calvin cycle reactions?
Think beyond just the core photosynthetic reactions to what the plant must do with the extra product - converting it, storing it and moving it around - plus the danger of too much light.
To earn full credit, make each point concrete by naming an example, such as a photosynthetic enzyme, a protective pigment, or a product like sucrose, starch or amino acids.
walkthrough:
More Light Means More Photosynthesis to Support**
High light gives more energy for the light-dependent reactions and, in turn, more ATP and reduced NADP for the Calvin cycle. To use that capacity the plant needs to make more of the machinery, so it switches on genes for photosynthetic enzymes and chloroplast proteins such as Rubisco, ATP synthase or photosystem proteins.

More Product Means More Processing and Transport**
Faster photosynthesis makes more triose phosphate, so the plant also needs enzymes to convert it to useful products such as sucrose, starch and amino acids, and carrier proteins to load sucrose and amino acids into phloem for transport to growing tissues.

More Light Means More Need for Protection**
Very high light can damage photosystems, so genes for protective pigments such as carotenoids / xanthophylls are also switched on. Together this explains why 14% of genes are on only in high light, compared with only 4% needed specifically for low-light survival.

Final answer: In high light intensity the plant can photosynthesise more, so upregulates genes for more photosynthetic enzymes / proteins e.g. Rubisco, ATP synthase, photosystem proteins; plus protective pigments against excess light; plus enzymes for making sucrose / starch / amino acids and transport proteins for sucrose / amino acids.
